deck.title: German Syllable, Length, and Stress
deck.sub: How a German word is divided, which vowels are long, and where the stress falls

panels.h: The German syllable and vowel length. A German syllable has one vowel or diphthong, and ei, au, eu, and äu are diphthongs: Bau-er has two syllables. A German vowel is long or short, and the spelling usually shows which. A vowel is long when it is doubled, as in See, when it is followed by a silent h, as in Sohn, when it is written ie, as in Liebe, and usually when one consonant follows it, as in Tag. A vowel before a doubled consonant is short, as in Mann and Bett.

q.prompt: Is the vowel of Mann long or short?
options: Short, because a doubled consonant follows
Long, because the word has one syllable
Short, because it is a noun
q.explain: A doubled consonant after a vowel shows that the vowel is short. Compare Sohn, where the silent h shows a long vowel.

panels.h: German stress. German does not use the Latin law of the penult. The stress falls on the first syllable of the stem, the main part of the word without a prefix: SPRE-chen, and in the participle ge-SPRO-chen, where ge- is not part of the stem. The inseparable prefixes be-, ge-, er-, ver-, and zer- are never stressed: ver-STE-hen. A separable prefix takes the stress: AN-kommen.

q.prompt: Where is the stress in gesprochen?
options: On the penult because it is long
q.explain: The stem of the participle is -sproch-, and ge- is an unstressed prefix.

panels.h: Compounds and borrowed words. A compound is usually stressed on its first part: HAUS-tür, BAHN-hof. Many borrowed words keep a stress of their own: verbs in -ieren are stressed on that ending, as in stu-DIE-ren, and nouns in -ität and -ei on the last syllable, as in U-ni-ver-si-TÄT and Bä-cke-REI.

q.prompt: Where is the stress in studieren?
q.explain: Verbs in -ieren are stressed on -ie-.

panels.h: Final devoicing. At the end of a word or a syllable, b, d, and g are pronounced as p, t, and k, although the spelling keeps b, d, and g: Tag ends with the sound k, and Hund with t. The spelling shows the sound of the other forms, where a vowel follows: Tage, Hunde.

q.prompt: How is the final d of Hund pronounced?
q.explain: At the end of a word, d is pronounced as t. In Hunde, where a vowel follows, it is a d.
